claim: UDP activates P2Y14 with an EC50 value of 50.9±6.1 nM
source: Both UDP and UDP-Glc potently activate P2Y14 with EC50 values of 50.9±6.1 nM and 40.3±1.5 nM, respectively (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental calcium mobilization assay data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1.

claim: UDP-Glc activates P2Y14 with an EC50 value of 40.3±1.5 nM
source: Both UDP and UDP-Glc potently activate P2Y14 with EC50 values of 50.9±6.1 nM and 40.3±1.5 nM, respectively (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental calcium mobilization assay data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1.

claim: UDP-Glc shows increased potency on P2Y14 at high concentration compared with UDP
source: Compared with UDP, UDP-Glc showed an increased potency on P2Y14 at high concentration (Figure 1B–C), suggesting that the sugar moiety of UDP-Glc contributes to activating P2Y14.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C comparing concentration-response curves.

claim: The sugar moiety of UDP-Glc contributes to activating P2Y14
source: Compared with UDP, UDP-Glc showed an increased potency on P2Y14 at high concentration (Figure 1B–C), suggesting that the sugar moiety of UDP-Glc contributes to activating P2Y14.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that UDP-Glc shows increased potency compared to UDP.

claim: Both UDP and UDP-Glc bind to an extracellular pocket consisting of TM helices 2–7 and extracellular loop (ECL) 2
source: The molecular docking showed that both UDP and UDP-Glc bind to an extracellular pocket consisting of TM helices 2–7 and extracellular loop (ECL) 2 (Figure 1D), which is corresponding to a known agonist binding pocket of P2Y12 (Zhang et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular docking simulations and comparison with known P2Y12 structures.

claim: The docking score of UDP-Glc is –9.3 kcal/mol
source: The docking score of UDP-Glc is –9.3 kcal/mol, and that of UDP is –8.5 kcal/mol, indicating that both UDP and UDP-Glc bind to P2Y14.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational docking calculations.

claim: The docking score of UDP is –8.5 kcal/mol
source: The docking score of UDP-Glc is –9.3 kcal/mol, and that of UDP is –8.5 kcal/mol, indicating that both UDP and UDP-Glc bind to P2Y14.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational docking calculations.

claim: Five residues (K772.60, D812.64, N903.21, I170ECL2, and E2787.36) stabilize UDP-Glc binding
source: Five residues (K772.60, D812.64, N903.21, I170ECL2, and E2787.36; superscript indicates Ballesteros-Weinstein residue numbering; Ballesteros and Weinstein, 1995) were predicted to stabilize UDP-Glc binding (Figure 1F and G), while they made few energetic contributions (van der Waals energy >–0.25 Rosetta energy unit) to UDP binding (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by energy decomposition analysis from molecular docking.

claim: K772.60, D812.64, N903.21, I170ECL2, and E2787.36 make few energetic contributions to UDP binding
source: Five residues (K772.60, D812.64, N903.21, I170ECL2, and E2787.36; superscript indicates Ballesteros-Weinstein residue numbering; Ballesteros and Weinstein, 1995) were predicted to stabilize UDP-Glc binding (Figure 1F and G), while they made few energetic contributions (van der Waals energy >–0.25 Rosetta energy unit) to UDP binding (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by energy decomposition analysis from molecular docking.

claim: D81A mutation significantly reduces P2Y14 activities by UDP-Glc compared with wild-type
source: Among these mutants, D81A showed significantly reduced activities by UDP-Glc compared with the wild-type (WT) group (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: D81A mutation does not significantly affect receptor activities by UDP
source: However, substitution of D812.64 by alanine did not significantly affect the receptor activities by UDP (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: K77A mutation diminishes both UDP-Glc- and UDP-induced calcium mobilization
source: Interestingly, K77A mutation diminished both UDP-Glc- and UDP-induced calcium mobilization (Figure 1H), but it showed greater impact on UDP-Glc-induced receptor responses than UDP-induced ones (Figure 1H, I), suggesting extra interactions between K772.60 and sugar moiety of UDP-Glc.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: K77A mutation shows greater impact on UDP-Glc-induced receptor responses than UDP-induced ones
source: Interestingly, K77A mutation diminished both UDP-Glc- and UDP-induced calcium mobilization (Figure 1H), but it showed greater impact on UDP-Glc-induced receptor responses than UDP-induced ones (Figure 1H, I), suggesting extra interactions between K772.60 and sugar moiety of UDP-Glc.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: K772.60 has extra interactions with the sugar moiety of UDP-Glc
source: Interestingly, K77A mutation diminished both UDP-Glc- and UDP-induced calcium mobilization (Figure 1H), but it showed greater impact on UDP-Glc-induced receptor responses than UDP-induced ones (Figure 1H, I), suggesting extra interactions between K772.60 and sugar moiety of UDP-Glc.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects of K77A mutation on UDP-Glc versus UDP responses.

claim: N90A and I170A mutations do not significantly affect receptor responses by UDP or UDP-Glc
source: Two mutations on TM3 and ECL2 (N90A and I170A) did not significantly affect the receptor responses by UDP or UDP-Glc (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: Sub-pocket 2 residues of TM2 provide major contributions to stabilizing the sugar moiety of UDP-Glc
source: These findings indicate that sub-pocket 2 residues of TM2 provide major contributions to stabilizing the sugar moiety of UDP-Glc.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined computational and experimental mutagenesis results.

claim: In UDP-Glc-bound P2Y14 simulations, the extracellular tip of TM6 shifted over 3 Å toward the receptor core compared with apo P2Y14 simulations
source: In UDP-Glc-bound P2Y14 simulations, the extracellular tip of TM6 shifted over 3 Å and TM7 over 4 Å toward the receptor core, compared with the apo P2Y14 simulations (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: In UDP-Glc-bound P2Y14 simulations, TM7 shifted over 4 Å toward the receptor core compared with apo P2Y14 simulations
source: In UDP-Glc-bound P2Y14 simulations, the extracellular tip of TM6 shifted over 3 Å and TM7 over 4 Å toward the receptor core, compared with the apo P2Y14 simulations (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: K2777.35 and E2787.36 form hydrogen bonds with the glucose 6' hydroxyl group of UDP-Glc during UDP-Glc-bound P2Y14 simulations
source: During UDP-Glc-bound P2Y14 simulations, two charged residues K2777.35 and E2787.36 formed hydrogen bonds with the glucose 6' hydroxyl group of UDP-Glc to keep TM7 close to the receptor core (Figure 2B and C), and an arginine residue (R2536.55) formed a salt bridge with the phosphate group of UDP-Glc to stabilize the inward shift of TM6 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: R2536.55 forms a salt bridge with the phosphate group of UDP-Glc to stabilize the inward shift of TM6
source: During UDP-Glc-bound P2Y14 simulations, two charged residues K2777.35 and E2787.36 formed hydrogen bonds with the glucose 6' hydroxyl group of UDP-Glc to keep TM7 close to the receptor core (Figure 2B and C), and an arginine residue (R2536.55) formed a salt bridge with the phosphate group of UDP-Glc to stabilize the inward shift of TM6 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: R253A mutation results in diminished UDP-Glc-induced calcium mobilization with EC50 of 808.6±43.6 nM compared with WT EC50 of 40.3±1.5 nM
source: Consistently, compared with WT group (EC50 of 40.3±1.5 nM), single-point mutations (R253A and E278A) of TM6 and TM7 helices resulted to diminished UDP-Glc-induced calcium mobilization (EC50 of 808.6±43.6 nM for R253A and 60.2±3.6 nM for E278A) (Figure 1H, Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: E278A mutation results in diminished UDP-Glc-induced calcium mobilization with EC50 of 60.2±3.6 nM compared with WT EC50 of 40.3±1.5 nM
source: Consistently, compared with WT group (EC50 of 40.3±1.5 nM), single-point mutations (R253A and E278A) of TM6 and TM7 helices resulted to diminished UDP-Glc-induced calcium mobilization (EC50 of 808.6±43.6 nM for R253A and 60.2±3.6 nM for E278A) (Figure 1H, Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: The distance between TM5 and TM6 of UDP-Glc-bound P2Y14 was 5.9 Å shorter than that in the apo system at the extracellular side
source: In addition, at the extracellular side, the distance between TM5 and TM6 of UDP-Glc-bound P2Y14 was 5.9 Å shorter than that in the apo system (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Y1895.41 and T2576.59 make stable hydrophobic interactions to maintain tight compact between TM5 and TM6 in UDP-Glc-bound-P2Y14 simulations
source: Y1895.41 and T2576.59 made stable hydrophobic interactions to maintain the tight compact between TM5 and TM6 in UDP-Glc-bound-P2Y14 simulations, while TM6 did not interact with TM5 at the extracellular side in the apo simulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: T257A mutation shows significantly reduced UDP-Glc-induced responses with EC50 of 504.9±15.9 nM compared with WT EC50 of 40.3±1.5 nM
source: Compared with WT group (EC50 of 40.3±1.5 nM), a mutation of TM6 (T257A) showed significantly reduced UDP-Glc-induced responses (EC50 of 504.9±15.9 nM) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), fully agreeing with our simulation models.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: UDP-Glc might serve as intramolecular 'glue' to make a tight helical bundle of P2Y14, involving TM6 and TM7
source: Collectively, these data suggest that UDP-Glc might serve as intramolecular 'glue' to make a tight helical bundle of P2Y14, involving TM6 and TM7.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined computational and experimental results showing conformational changes and interactions.

claim: UDP-Glc induces activity on P2Y14 with EC50 of 40.3 ± 1.5 nM
source: With only one group substitution at the sugar moiety, UDP-Glc induced stronger activity on P2Y14 (EC50=40.3 ± 1.5 nM) than the other UDP-sugars, that is, UDP-Gal (EC50=78.3 ± 9.2 nM), UDP-GlcA (EC50=59.9 ± 4.8 nM), and UDP-GlcNAc (EC50=184.4 ± 11.8 nM) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: UDP-Gal induces activity on P2Y14 with EC50 of 78.3 ± 9.2 nM
source: With only one group substitution at the sugar moiety, UDP-Glc induced stronger activity on P2Y14 (EC50=40.3 ± 1.5 nM) than the other UDP-sugars, that is, UDP-Gal (EC50=78.3 ± 9.2 nM), UDP-GlcA (EC50=59.9 ± 4.8 nM), and UDP-GlcNAc (EC50=184.4 ± 11.8 nM) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: UDP-GlcA induces activity on P2Y14 with EC50 of 59.9 ± 4.8 nM
source: With only one group substitution at the sugar moiety, UDP-Glc induced stronger activity on P2Y14 (EC50=40.3 ± 1.5 nM) than the other UDP-sugars, that is, UDP-Gal (EC50=78.3 ± 9.2 nM), UDP-GlcA (EC50=59.9 ± 4.8 nM), and UDP-GlcNAc (EC50=184.4 ± 11.8 nM) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc induces activity on P2Y14 with EC50 of 184.4 ± 11.8 nM
source: With only one group substitution at the sugar moiety, UDP-Glc induced stronger activity on P2Y14 (EC50=40.3 ± 1.5 nM) than the other UDP-sugars, that is, UDP-Gal (EC50=78.3 ± 9.2 nM), UDP-GlcA (EC50=59.9 ± 4.8 nM), and UDP-GlcNAc (EC50=184.4 ± 11.8 nM) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: A stable salt bridging chain formed by K772.60, D812.64, K2777.35, and E2787.36 was observed in all UDP-sugar-bound P2Y14 simulation systems
source: At the sub-pocket 2, a stable salt bridging chain formed by four charged residues (K772.60, D812.64, K2777.35, and E2787.36) were observed in all systems (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: E2787.36 links TM2 and TM7 helices by forming salt bridges with K772.60 and K2777.35
source: The negative charged glutamic acid residue E2787.36 linked TM2 and TM7 helices by forming salt bridges with K772.60 and K2777.35, while the other negative charged residue D812.64 forming a salt bridge with K772.60 to further stabilize these ionic interactions (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: D812.64 forms a salt bridge with K772.60 to further stabilize ionic interactions
source: The negative charged glutamic acid residue E2787.36 linked TM2 and TM7 helices by forming salt bridges with K772.60 and K2777.35, while the other negative charged residue D812.64 forming a salt bridge with K772.60 to further stabilize these ionic interactions (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: In UDP-GlcA-bound P2Y14 simulations, the 5' carboxyl group of the sugar moiety fails to form hydrogen bond with E2787.36
source: However, in UDP-GlcA-bound P2Y14 simulations, at the corresponding position, the 5' carboxyl group of the sugar moiety failed to form hydrogen bond with the negatively charged E2787.36 (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: E278A mutation does not decrease UDP-GlcA-induced calcium mobilization with EC50 of 38.2 ± 2.2 nM compared with WT EC50 of 59.9 ± 4.8 nM
source: Compared with that of WT group (EC50=59.9 ± 4.8 nM), the single-point mutation of E278A did not decrease the UDP-GlcA-induced calcium mobilization (EC50=38.2 ± 2.2 nM) (Figure 3G), supporting with the proposed sugar-binding model (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: Substitution of 2' hydroxyl group by an acetamido group leads to a rotation of the sugar moiety of UDP-GlcNAc in simulations
source: Substitution of 2' hydroxyl group by an acetamido group led to a rotation of the sugar moiety of UDP-GlcNAc in simulations (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The 6' hydroxyl of N-acetylglucosamine group flips to form hydrogen bonds with K772.60 and D812.64 instead of K2777.35 and E2787.36
source: Consequentially, the 6' hydroxyl of N-acetylglucosamine group flipped to form hydrogen bonds with K772.60 and D812.64 instead of K2777.35 and E2787.36 (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: D81A mutation makes significant effect to reduce UDP-GlcNAc-induced receptor activities
source: Consistently, single-point mutation of D81A made significant effect to reduce the UDP-GlcNAc-induced receptor activities (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: The 4' hydroxyl group of galactose forms a stable hydrogen bond with K772.60
source: Compared with the other three UDP-sugars, UDP-Gal has a different orientation of 4' hydroxyl group. The 4' hydroxyl group of galactose formed a stable hydrogen bond with K772.60 and disrupted the interaction between 6' hydroxyl group with E2787.36 (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The 4' hydroxyl group of galactose disrupts the interaction between 6' hydroxyl group with E2787.36
source: Compared with the other three UDP-sugars, UDP-Gal has a different orientation of 4' hydroxyl group. The 4' hydroxyl group of galactose formed a stable hydrogen bond with K772.60 and disrupted the interaction between 6' hydroxyl group with E2787.36 (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: E278A mutation does not significantly affect UDP-Gal-induced receptor response
source: Substitution of E2787.36 by alanine did not significantly affect the UDP-Gal-induced receptor response (Figure 3I), agreeing with the proposed UDP-Gal-binding model (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: For all UDP-sugars, at least three residues of K772.60, D812.64, K2777.35, and E2787.36 participate in ligand binding
source: For all UDP-sugars, at least three residues of K772.60, D812.64, K2777.35, and E2787.36 participated in ligand binding (Figure 2, Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data and mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The K772.60-D812.64-K2777.35-E2787.36 salt bridging chain is a sugar-binding site of P2Y14 that can recognize different sugar moieties
source: Both computational models and experimental data indicate the K772.60-D812.64-K2777.35-E2787.36 salt bridging chain as a sugar-binding site of P2Y14, which can recognize different sugar moieties.
evidence: The claim is supported by combined computational and experimental evidence.

claim: The interactions of ligands with TM7 might determine the ligand potency on P2Y14
source: The interactions of ligands with the TM7 might determine the ligand potency on P2Y14.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential binding modes and potencies of various UDP-sugars.

claim: K2.60, D2.64, K7.35, and E7.36 are conserved between P2Y14 and P2Y12
source: These four residues (K2.60, D2.64, K7.35, and E7.36) are conserved between P2Y14 and its closest homolog, that is, P2Y12 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: P2Y12 is activated by ADP
source: P2Y12 is activated by ADP (Herbert and Savi, 2003), but it has not been reported to be activated by any sugar nucleotide.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: P2Y12 has not been reported to be activated by any sugar nucleotide
source: P2Y12 is activated by ADP (Herbert and Savi, 2003), but it has not been reported to be activated by any sugar nucleotide.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of reports in the literature.

claim: The docking score for ADP-Glc to P2Y12 is –9.4 kcal/mol
source: The docking scores are –9.4 kcal/mol for ADP-Glc, for –10.0 kcal/mol for ADP-GlcA, and –9.3 kcal/mol for ADP-Man (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting they stably bound to P2Y12.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational docking calculations.

claim: The docking score for ADP-GlcA to P2Y12 is –10.0 kcal/mol
source: The docking scores are –9.4 kcal/mol for ADP-Glc, for –10.0 kcal/mol for ADP-GlcA, and –9.3 kcal/mol for ADP-Man (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting they stably bound to P2Y12.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational docking calculations.

claim: The docking score for ADP-Man to P2Y12 is –9.3 kcal/mol
source: The docking scores are –9.4 kcal/mol for ADP-Glc, for –10.0 kcal/mol for ADP-GlcA, and –9.3 kcal/mol for ADP-Man (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting they stably bound to P2Y12.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational docking calculations.

claim: ADP-Glc activates P2Y12 with EC50 of 3.4±0.4 μM
source: Consistently, in calcium mobilization assays, ADP-Glc, ADP-GlcA, and ADP-Man activated P2Y12 with EC50 values of 3.4±0.4 μM, 1.3±0.1 μM, and 12.3±0.9 μM, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: ADP-GlcA activates P2Y12 with EC50 of 1.3±0.1 μM
source: Consistently, in calcium mobilization assays, ADP-Glc, ADP-GlcA, and ADP-Man activated P2Y12 with EC50 values of 3.4±0.4 μM, 1.3±0.1 μM, and 12.3±0.9 μM, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: ADP-Man activates P2Y12 with EC50 of 12.3±0.9 μM
source: Consistently, in calcium mobilization assays, ADP-Glc, ADP-GlcA, and ADP-Man activated P2Y12 with EC50 values of 3.4±0.4 μM, 1.3±0.1 μM, and 12.3±0.9 μM, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: Single-point mutations of K802.60, D842.64, K2807.35, and E2817.36 significantly diminish ADP-Glc-, ADP-GlcA-, and ADP-Man-induced responses compared with WT P2Y12
source: Single-point mutations of K802.60, D842.64, K2807.35, and E2817.36 significantly diminished ADP-Glc-, ADP-GlcA-, and ADP-Man-induced responses, compared with WT P2Y12 (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: The KDKE salt bridging chain is a conserved functional motif for sugar binding in both P2Y14 and P2Y12
source: These findings not only validate our assumption that P2Y12 can be activated by sugar nucleotides, but also indicate the conserved KDKE salt bridging chain as a functional motif for sugar binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by combined computational and experimental evidence from both receptors.

claim: F2777.32 is a less conserved residue adjacent to the KDKE motif of P2Y12
source: In addition, we found a less conserved phenylalanine residue F2777.32, which is adjacent to the KDKE motif of P2Y12 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and structural modeling.

claim: F277A mutation significantly reduces ADP-Glc-induced responses of P2Y12 compared with WT
source: The alanine substitution of F2777.32 significantly reduced ADP-Glc-induced responses of P2Y12, compared with that of the WT group (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: Single-point mutations at the corresponding position of P2Y14 do not significantly affect UDP-Glc-induced activation
source: However, single-point mutations at the corresponding position of P2Y14 did not significantly affect the UDP-Glc-induced activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental mutagenesis and calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: P2Y14 belongs to P2Y purinoceptor subfamily consisting of receptors responding to nucleotides including ADP and UDP
source: It belongs to P2Y purinoceptor subfamily, consisting of receptors responding to nucleotides, including adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and UDP (Ralevic and Burnstock, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: P2Y14 is potently activated by UDP and UDP-sugars
source: Distinct from the other purinoceptors, P2Y14 is potently activated by UDP and a class of carbohydrates, that is, UDP-sugars (Abbracchio et al., 2006; Jacobson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: UDP-sugars activate P2Y14 with a relative potency order of UDP-glucose, UDP-galactose, UDP-glucuronic acid, and UDP-N-acetylglucosamine
source: UDP-sugars activate P2Y14 with a relative potency order of UDP-glucose (UDP-Glc), UDP-galactose (UDP-Gal), UDP-glucuronic acid (UDP-GlcA), and UDP-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc) (Chambers et al., 2000; Hamel et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2009; Ko et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: UDP-Glc regulates immune responses and associates with asthma, kidney injury, and lung inflammation
source: Particularly, UDP-Glc regulates immune responses and associate with asthma, kidney injury, and lung inflammation (Amison et al., 2017; Breton and Brown, 2018; Ferreira et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2005; Sesma et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: UDP-Gal is present in various cell models including physiologically relevant primary cultures of human bronchial epithelial cells
source: As an isomer of UDP-Glc, UDP-Gal is present in various cell models, including physiologically relevant primary cultures of human bronchial epithelial cells (Lazarowski, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: P2Y12 is the closest homolog to P2Y14
source: As the closest homolog to P2Y14, P2Y purinoceptor 12 (P2Y12) has not been reported to be activated by any sugar nucleotide (Jacobson et al., 2020; Ralevic and Burnstock, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: P2Y12 has 45.67% amino acid sequence identity with P2Y14
source: Since P2Y12 is highly similar to P2Y14 with 45.67% amino acid sequence identity, it would be interesting to investigate whether this receptor is also sensible to sugar nucleotides.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Carbohydrates play indispensable roles in energy supply, cell signaling, and immune responses
source: As significant components of the organism, carbohydrates play indispensable roles in energy supply, cell signaling, and immune responses (Gagneux and Varki, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulation of carbohydrates has been proved to be associated with the development of various diseases
source: Dysregulation of carbohydrates has been proved to be associated with the development of various diseases (Reily et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: P2Y14 plays an important role in immune responses and inflammation mediated by UDP-sugars
source: Mediated by UDP-sugars, P2Y14 plays an important role in immune responses and inflammation (Arase et al., 2009; Barrett et al., 2013; Breton and Brown, 2018; Ferreira et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2005; Sesma et al., 2012; Sesma et al., 2016), and possibly insulin resistance (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: P2Y14 possibly plays a role in insulin resistance
source: Mediated by UDP-sugars, P2Y14 plays an important role in immune responses and inflammation (Arase et al., 2009; Barrett et al., 2013; Breton and Brown, 2018; Ferreira et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2005; Sesma et al., 2012; Sesma et al., 2016), and possibly insulin resistance (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature with speculative language.

claim: Kidney collecting duct intercalated cells present high levels of P2Y14
source: Breton et al. found that kidney collecting duct intercalated cells present high levels of P2Y14, which is activated by UDP-Glc to promote neutrophil infiltration and renal inflammation (Breton and Brown, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: P2Y14 is activated by UDP-Glc to promote neutrophil infiltration and renal inflammation
source: Breton et al. found that kidney collecting duct intercalated cells present high levels of P2Y14, which is activated by UDP-Glc to promote neutrophil infiltration and renal inflammation (Breton and Brown, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: High concentration of UDP-sugars was observed in extracellular tissue surrounding airway epithelial cells and lung secretions of cystic fibrosis patients
source: Exerting excessive P2Y14-mediated inflammatory reactions, high concentration of UDP-sugars was observed in extracellular tissue surrounding airway epithelial cells and lung secretions of cystic fibrosis patients (Ferreira et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2005; Sesma et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: UDP-Glc is released from liver cells in obese states possibly via hepatocellular apoptosis leading to liver inflammation and insulin resistance
source: UDP-Glc is also released from liver cells in obese states, possibly via hepatocellular apoptosis, leading to liver inflammation and insulin resistance (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature with speculative language about the mechanism.

claim: The agonist-induced conformational changes of TM6 and TM7 are reported for P2Y12
source: The agonist-induced remarkable conformational changes of TM6 and TM7 are also reported for P2Y12 (Zhang et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In the 2MeSADP-bound P2Y12 structure, the extracellular part of TM6 shifts over 10 Å toward the center of TM helix bundle compared with the AZD1283-bound P2Y12 structure
source: Compared with the AZD1283-bound (antagonist-bound) P2Y12 structure (Zhang et al., 2014b), the extracellular part of TM6 in the 2MeSADP-bound (agonist-bound) P2Y12 structure shifts over 10 Å and TM7 over 5 Å toward the center of TM helix bundle (Zhang et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature describing crystal structures.

claim: In the 2MeSADP-bound P2Y12 structure, TM7 shifts over 5 Å toward the center of TM helix bundle compared with the AZD1283-bound P2Y12 structure
source: Compared with the AZD1283-bound (antagonist-bound) P2Y12 structure (Zhang et al., 2014b), the extracellular part of TM6 in the 2MeSADP-bound (agonist-bound) P2Y12 structure shifts over 10 Å and TM7 over 5 Å toward the center of TM helix bundle (Zhang et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature describing crystal structures.

claim: The close parallel of P2Y12 and P2Y14 in agonist-induced conformational changes indicates a common ligand-induced activation mechanism shared by purinergic receptors
source: The close parallel of P2Y12 and P2Y14 in the agonist-induced conformational changes indicates a common ligand-induced activation mechanism shared by purinergic receptors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing conformational changes in both receptors.

claim: P2Y13 has the conserved KDKE site
source: As another member of P2Y12-like subfamily, P2Y13 also has the conserved KDKE site (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting it might be regulated by carbohydrates.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: P2Y13 might be regulated by carbohydrates
source: As another member of P2Y12-like subfamily, P2Y13 also has the conserved KDKE site (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting it might be regulated by carbohydrates.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the presence of the conserved KDKE motif.

claim: GPR87 is a close homolog of P2Y14 with sequence identity of 44.94%
source: GPR87 is a close homolog of P2Y14 with the sequence identity of 44.94%.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: GPR87 has K/R2.60, D2.64, K/E7.35, and E7.36 at the corresponding positions of the KDKE sugar-binding motif
source: GPR87 has K/R2.60, D2.64, K/E7.35, and E7.36 at the corresponding positions of the KDKE sugar-binding motif, indicating varied carbohydrate sensitivities of this receptor in different species (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: GPR87 shows varied carbohydrate sensitivities in different species
source: GPR87 has K/R2.60, D2.64, K/E7.35, and E7.36 at the corresponding positions of the KDKE sugar-binding motif, indicating varied carbohydrate sensitivities of this receptor in different species (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the sequence variation at the KDKE motif positions.

claim: Selective mono-fluorination of the 6' hydroxyl group of the glucose moiety results in fourfold less potency on P2Y14
source: Consistent with our observations, a previous structure-activity relationship study revealed that selective mono-fluorination of the 6' hydroxyl group of the glucose moiety results to fourfold less potency on P2Y14 (Ko et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: UDP-sugar-binding sites consisting of charged residues have been discovered for sugar transferases
source: Similar to the KDKE motif of the receptors, the UDP-sugar-binding sites consisting of charged residues have been discovered for sugar transferases (Gerlach et al., 2018; Hao et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In typical glycosylation transfers as TarP and SseK3, two aspartic acids and one positively charged residue participate in recognition of 3' or 4' hydroxyl groups of GlcNAc or GalNAc moiety
source: In typical glycosylation transfers as TarP and SseK3, two aspartic acids and one positively charged residue (arginine or lysine) participate in recognition of 3' or 4' hydroxyl groups of GlcNAc or GalNAc moiety (Gerlach et al., 2018; Hao et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A salt bridging chain has not been observed in sugar-binding sites of sugar transferases
source: However, a salt bridging chain has not been observed in these sugar-binding sites.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of reports in the literature about sugar transferases.

claim: The different arrangements of UDP-sugar-binding sites between P2Y14 and sugar transferases might be determinant for their sugar selectivity
source: The different arrangements of UDP-sugar-binding sites between P2Y14 and these sugar transferases might be determinant for their sugar selectivity.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from comparing binding site architectures.

claim: A conserved carbohydrate-binding motif exists in both P2Y12 and P2Y14
source: In conclusion, we revealed a conserved carbohydrate-binding motif in both P2Y12 and P2Y14, extending our understanding of how carbohydrates regulate GPCRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined computational and experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: The molecular models of different sugar nucleotides provide details for carbohydrate activation and recognition of P2Y14 and P2Y12
source: Our molecular models of different sugar nucleotides provide great details for carbohydrate activation and recognition of these receptors, which would inspire further carbohydrate drug development for GPCRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the computational modeling and experimental validation presented in the manuscript.

claim: Whether other carbohydrate-binding motifs exist in GPCRs is currently unknown
source: Whether the other carbohydrate-binding motifs exist in GPCRs is currently unknown.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the limits of current knowledge.

claim: The crystal structures of P2Y12 show that 2MeSADP binds to an extracellular pocket consisting of transmembrane helices and extracellular loops
source: The crystal structures of P2Y12 show that a full agonist 2-methylthio-adenosine-5'-diphosphate (2MeSADP, a close analogue of ADP) binds to an extracellular pocket consisting of transmembrane (TM) helices and extracellular loops (Zhang et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature describing crystal structures.

claim: UDP-sugars act as important signaling molecules via P2Y14 to mediate many physiological processes
source: These sugar nucleotides act as important signaling molecules via P2Y14 to mediate many physiological processes (Amison et al., 2017; Breton and Brown, 2018; Ferreira et al., 2017; Lazarowski, 2010; Müller et al., 2005; Sesma et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.
